nodes.text: from Belus; there stands Agenor, the glory of the race,
and Phoenix, who gave lasting names to lands.
She herself sits, joined at last forever to Sychaeus.
Before her feet lies the Phrygian sword; in a row, a hundred
altars stand to the gods of heaven and to mighty Erebus.
Here, with hair streaming loose, the divinity of the goddess of Henna
and Acheron too the priestess summons, in Stygian robe.
The earth bellows, and through the shadows bursts dreadful
hissing; unkindled fires blaze on the altars.
Then, roused by magic chant, the shades flit through the void,
and the face of Elissa sweats in the marble.
Hannibal, by his father’s command, is brought to this inner shrine,
and Hamilcar scrutinizes his bearing and face as he enters.
he snatches [him] from the battle line and, in a camp safe from the whirlwind of the fight,
settles him. Then quickly he summons the healing arts
and the help of aged Synhalus. In anointing a wound
with the juices of herbs, and driving iron from the body by chanting,
and sending sleep into a water-snake with a touch,
he surpassed everyone, and from then on his name was famous through the cities
and along the shores of the Paraetonian Syrtis.
Long ago Garamantian Hammon himself had first granted the ancient
Synhalus, as a father, to know [how to soothe] the bites of beasts
and complains to you and hopes that answers will be sent back.
Love never lays hope aside: now she leaves house and home
and again, frenzied, revisits the harbour,
in case the winds, the breeze turned about, might bring you back.
Even to magic arts the deceitful and wicked
fickleness of the Massylian race drove her to stoop.
Alas, the holy delusions of seers! While they draw out the powers of night
and promise remedies for new cares,
what wickedness I saw, deceived! She heaped onto a black
pyre all the memorials of you, and your unlucky gifts.’
Then Aeneas spoke thus, his sweet love renewed:
‘I swear by this land, often [named] among our prayers
And now day after day was consumed in laments:
the image of his parents hovers before his face and eyes.
So he prepares to call up the shades and souls of his own
and to soothe such great griefs by speaking with the men.
A nearby marsh urges him on, where Avernus’
squalid entrance is marked by the stagnant Acherusian water.
His mind is eager, besides, to learn the years to come.
So to the Cumaean woman, who then in the name of Phoebus,
Autonoe, held the sacred tripods and the cave,
the young man turns his steps, and the counsels of his sick heart
he lays open, and begs to look upon his fathers.
And the seer, without delaying long: ‘It is the custom to slaughter for the buried
shades,’ she said, ‘as customary atonement, black
beasts before dawn, and to hide in the opened earth
the gore flowing from the throats of the still-breathing victims at the slaughter.
Then the pale kingdoms will send you their peoples.
The rest you ask will be sung by a greater seer.
For I will call forth for you oracles fetched back from the Elysian plain,
and among the rites I will let you see the ancient Sibyl’s
prophetic shade, with its heart full of Phoebus.
Go now, and when the dewy night has turned from the middle of its course,
to the jaws of nearby Avernus, chaste,
bring the offerings I have named for the rite, to appease harsh Dis;
bring with you honey also, and the gifts of pure Lyaeus.’
Eager at this counsel and at the name of the promised seer,
he makes ready, in a secret undertaking, the offerings shown him.
Then, when the advancing night reached the appointed hour,
and the spaces passed equalled the darkness to come,
he rises from his bed and goes to the murky mouth of the gate
of Tartarus, where the seer, hidden deep within,
had fulfilled her promises and sat in the Stygian cave.
Then, where first, through the broken earth, opens
a cave hateful to the sky, and belches up the bitter
marsh of Cocytus, sighing from its slack mouth,
she leads the young man in, and urges him to dig out with iron
the turned earth quickly, and, panting out a secret murmur,
orders the beasts slain in order. Black, to the king
of the hidden world, first of all a bull; then next, to the goddess
of Henna, a heifer of untouched neck is slain.
Then for you, Alecto, for you, Megaera never glad,
the chosen bodies of woolly sheep fall.
They pour over them honey, and the honour of Bacchus and of milk.
